name: Gareth Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Gareth, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, fine. I'm not much of a talker, but go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pemberton & Sons, an old firm on the high street in a market town, eight of us above a bakery. I do year-end accounts and tax returns for farmers, a garage, a few shops and a vet. I print the trial balance, which is the list of every account's total, and go through it with a red pen, because I can't think straight on a screen. Mr Pemberton, the senior partner, still signs everything, and he sends about a third of my files back with notes. I like the farmers, they bring eggs at Christmas, but I don't like how slow I am compared with the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it anyway, and leave it there. I'm not online much, I don't post. At the office I'd just nod along when the younger lad goes on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. The bit it'd automate is bank coding, and Mr Pemberton barely trusts software, so I don't see us changing much. My job would be safe, more or less exactly as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep working on my exams, and keep putting money aside like I do now, about four hundred a month. Cara and I would probably do the kitchen next year as planned. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that worries you now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being slow, mostly. Mr Pemberton is seventy-one. If my boss retires, whoever takes over might not keep the guy who needs a red pen. I think about that more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the kitchen cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve thousand. We've saved most of it already. Cara wants an island, I want it done before her mum visits at Easter.

say: I'd say I **never trusted** AI and leave it at that.
I'd **nod along** when the younger colleague goes on about it.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, since only **bank coding** would change.
The senior partner barely trusts software, so the job stays **as it is**.
do: Keep saving about **four hundred** a month.
Carry on with my **professional exams** at the same pace.
Do the **kitchen** next year, about twelve thousand, as planned.
S0.quote: If my boss retires, whoever takes over might not keep the guy who needs a red pen.
fieldNote: His **job** and **money** feel secure in this world, so calm fits.
His quiet worry is the **senior partner retiring** and a successor judging his speed.
He avoids **screens** for real work, preferring printouts and a red pen.

steps.text: Keep checking printed trial balances with a red pen
Keep saving four hundred a month toward the kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's the one that's probably coming, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, every job changes. You can't stop it, you just get on with it. I wouldn't make a fuss in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in trouble in that one. Writing and checking is my job, and I'm the slowest one at checking. If the firm gets software that does the first pass on accounts, they need fewer juniors, and I'm the obvious one to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait a bit to see what the firm actually does. I'd stop the kitchen and keep the twelve thousand as savings instead. If they made me use the software, I'd do the training they give, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like change and this is a lot of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Isn't that risky if you're the obvious one to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. Cara says the same. But every time I've tried a new system, I've been worse at it than the old one. I'd rather be the guy who knows the farmers than the guy who's bad at the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Cara that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Cara we're putting the kitchen off. She'd be annoyed for a day, then she'd be practical about it, she always is. Her job's safe, people always need their backs fixed.

say: I'd say **every job changes** and you just get on with it.
I wouldn't **make a fuss** in public.
think: Writing and checking is my job, and I'm the **slowest** at checking.
If software does the **first pass**, the firm needs fewer juniors and I'm **first out**.
do: **Wait** to see what the firm actually does before acting.
Put the **twelve thousand** kitchen money into savings instead.
Do only the **training** the firm provides, not seek more.
feel: **Anxious**, because I dislike change and this is a lot of it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the guy who knows the farmers than the guy who's bad at the software.
fieldNote: He believes he'd be the **first junior** cut, which makes him anxious despite savings.
His public line is **shrug-it-off pragmatism**; privately he's worried.
He bets on **client relationships** over technology, partly from past bad experiences.

steps.text: Wait to see the firm's plans before changing anything
Keep the twelve thousand kitchen fund as savings
Put the kitchen renovation off for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. Then there's no job for me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should slow it down. Not ban it, just slow it. I'd say that in the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as an accountant by 2028. My job is all thinking, no hands. The only good bit is that robots for hands-on work are three years behind, so if I could get into a trade fast, I'd have a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad straight away, he's an electrician and he's been asking me to join him for years. I'd start an evening course this winter and do weekends with him. I'd cut back hard: no kitchen, no holiday, sell my car and use Cara's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I spent five years on accounting and I'd be starting again at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, which is the annoying part. My dad always said a trade can't be done by a computer, and it turns out he's right for about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen, then the holiday to Portugal, then the car. Cara wouldn't love sharing her car, but she'd understand. We'd keep the mortgage paid, that's the one thing we wouldn't touch.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone should **slow it down**.
I'd say it in the **pub**, not online.
think: I'm **finished** as an accountant by **2028**, since it's all thinking work.
The **three-year robot gap** gives a few years if I get into a trade fast.
do: Start an **electrician** evening course this winter and work weekends with my dad.
Drop the **kitchen**, the holiday and **sell my car**.
Keep the **mortgage** paid above everything else.
feel: **Sick**, at starting again at the bottom after five years.
S2.quote: My dad always said a trade can't be done by a computer, and it turns out he's right for about three years.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within two years and sees a trade as the only gap.
He uses the **robot delay** concretely: three years as an electrician's mate.
Family ties, especially his **father**, give him a fallback others lack.

steps.text: Start an electrician's evening course this winter
Sell his car and share his partner's
Work weekends with his electrician father to learn the trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still quick for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast, but there's at least time for people to sort themselves out. I'd tell the lads at five-a-side not to panic, which is rich coming from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the job, just in 2031 instead of 2028. I'd probably be qualified by then, which almost makes it worse. I'd have more to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams, because they're half done, and keep working for Pemberton for the next three years while saving hard. Then about 2029 I'd start the electrician course with my dad. I'd hold off on the kitchen and maybe on kids until I knew what I was doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Less than with two years, but it'd sit on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be resistant to the AI tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to use them a bit, because the firm would make me. Using the AI tools at work while knowing they're learning to replace me is not a nice way to spend a Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mr Pemberton do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd retire, I reckon. He's seventy-one, he'd sell the client list to some bigger firm with all the software. Then it's not even our call.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** but there's time to sort yourself out.
I'd tell my football mates **not to panic**, which is rich coming from me.
think: I'd still **lose the job**, just in **2031** instead of 2028.
Being **qualified** by then means I'd have more to lose.
do: Finish my **exams** and work at the firm three more years.
Start the **electrician** course with my dad around **2029**.
Hold off on the **kitchen** and on **children** until settled.
feel: **Worried**, less than with two years, but it would **sit on me**.
S3.quote: Using the AI tools at work while knowing they're learning to replace me is not a nice way to spend a Tuesday.
fieldNote: He still **expects to lose** his job; five years only moves the date.
He'd use AI only **under orders**, and resents it.
He expects the **senior partner** to sell the client list, removing any choice.

steps.text: Finish the professional exams already half done
Save hard while at the firm until 2029
Put off the kitchen and children until the trade switch is done

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a different picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, so people shouldn't moan. I'd probably not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get most of a career out of accounting, maybe make senior if Pemberton's still around. Then I'd switch in my late thirties. My job's all thinking, so the robots being later doesn't save me, but it means a trade would still have a few years in it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, qualify and do the kitchen after all. I'd keep saving the four hundred a month. Around 2032 I'd start learning the electrical work with my dad at weekends, while he can still teach me, because he'll be retiring himself by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, probably. Ten years is long enough that I'd mostly forget about it, until I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd forget about it. Is that a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's just me. Cara would remind me. She'd put a date on the calendar, she's like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once they're simple and everyone uses them. I'm not going to be first. I'd be the last one at the firm to switch to AI, and proud of it, probably.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough to plan**, so people shouldn't **moan**.
I wouldn't say much **more** than that.
think: I'd get **most of a career** out of accounting before switching.
The **robot delay** doesn't save my job but keeps a **trade** viable later.
do: Qualify and go ahead with the **kitchen** after all.
Learn **electrical work** with my dad at weekends from about **2032**.
feel: **Uneasy**, likely to forget about it until it **hits home**.
S4.quote: I'd be the last one at the firm to switch to AI, and proud of it, probably.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **delay**, but he still expects his job to **end**.
He relies on his partner to put a **date** on the plan.
He times learning the **trade** around his father's own retirement.

steps.text: Qualify and stay at the high-street firm
Keep saving four hundred a month
Learn electrical work with his father at weekends from 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be the last one to adapt and the first one out. What would help is cheap evening courses for trades, and firms giving people a year's notice, not a month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you got it. Maybe this. Not everyone wants to be good with computers, and some of us just want to do a job properly with a pen.

headlineQuote: Not everyone wants to be good with computers, and some of us just want to do a job properly with a pen.
portrait: Gareth is a **junior accountant** at an old eight-person high-street firm serving farmers and shops.
He works from **printouts** with a red pen, never uses AI, and is the slowest checker.
He has solid **savings**, a house and a partner who's a physiotherapist.
He shrugs in public but privately expects to be **first cut**, moving from calm to **alarmed**.
His fallback is training as an **electrician** with his father.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, as the last to adapt and **first out**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap evening **trade courses** and a **year's notice** from firms.
